title: The Oresteia
author: Aeschylus
openingText:
A WATCHMAN. I pray the gods to release me from this labor, to end the watch I have kept this whole long year. Lying like a watchdog with no real rest, propped on one arm upon the palace roof of the house of Atreus, too long and too well I have come to know the starry council of the midnight sky — too well, the splendors of the firmament, those royal lords of light whose movements, as they rise and set in turn, mark out the seasons of the year, bringing frost or fire.

And now, as always, I am stationed here to watch for the moment when the signal-flame will blaze up — the beacon-fire that will tell its Trojan tale: _Troy is taken._ So she hopes, the one with a woman's body and a man's heart beating in her breast.
about:
The Oresteia comprises Agamemnon, The Libation Bearers and The Eumenides. A king returns from war and is killed by his wife. Their son avenges him on Apollo’s orders, then faces pursuit for killing his mother. Each side claims justice.

In the final play Athena appoints citizens of Athens to judge Orestes. She gives her own vote to him and establishes that an equal vote means acquittal. After the verdict she must still negotiate with the Furies. Follow both the new court and the older powers that receive a place in the city. The trial also includes explicit arguments for the father’s precedence over the mother.

This reading edition modernizes E. D. A. Morshead’s English translation. Its 26 reading sections divide the three plays for navigation. Images, choral songs and stage action carry the arguments together.

angleCards.title: Revenge and judgment
angleCards.text: Follow the reasons offered for each killing and how the next act of revenge grows from it. Ask what the trial changes and what still requires negotiation.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to compare the reasons the parties give for violence and judgment.

angleCards.title: Clytemnestra’s arguments
angleCards.text: Clytemnestra invokes Iphigenia’s sacrifice to defend her killing. Consider her treatment of Cassandra and Orestes too, and test her reasons for yourself.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to examine the relationship between Clytemnestra’s grief, power and actions.

angleCards.title: A place for the Furies
angleCards.text: The Furies demand punishment for killing a mother. After the acquittal they threaten the land. Notice how Athena uses offers, persuasion and power in negotiating with them.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to follow what the Furies relinquish and what they receive.

angleCards.title: Cassandra’s foresight
angleCards.text: Cassandra speaks of the household’s past and her approaching death. The Chorus responds with understanding, questions and confusion. Follow where their conversation succeeds and where it breaks down.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to read Cassandra’s speeches alongside the Chorus’s responses.

cast.name: Agamemnon
cast.description: He returns from the Trojan War. His sacrifice of his daughter Iphigenia is central to Clytemnestra’s accusation against him.

cast.name: Clytemnestra
cast.description: Agamemnon’s wife and Orestes’ mother. She has taken Aegisthus as her lover and invokes past wrongs to defend killing her husband.

cast.name: Cassandra
cast.description: Agamemnon brings her home as a captive. She sees the household’s past and her own approaching death and tries to share her knowledge with the Chorus.

cast.name: Orestes
cast.description: He returns to avenge his father. Apollo’s command drives him, but killing his mother makes him the Furies’ prey.

cast.name: The Furies
cast.description: Daughters of Night who pursue those who kill their kin. They prosecute Orestes, then negotiate a home and an honoured role in Athens.

cast.name: Athena
cast.description: She establishes the court, votes for Orestes and sets the rule of acquittal on an equal vote. Afterwards she seeks reconciliation between the city and the Furies.

whyItMatters.title: Justice on stage
whyItMatters.body: The trial lets readers compare competing claims to justice. Consider the evidence, the gods’ power and the arguments about gender and kinship used in reaching judgment.

whyItMatters.title: A family’s inheritance
whyItMatters.body: Past killings keep shaping the choices of the living. Recurring images of nets, blood and pursuit connect the three plays.

whyItMatters.title: The price of reconciliation
whyItMatters.body: The verdict ends the trial, but the city remains under threat. The final agreement asks how a new order can make room for older powers.
